name: Nikhil Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A normal week is four days of lectures in computer science, mostly programming, logic and a maths module I'm finding tougher than I expected. I live in a flat share with three others above a kebab shop, which smells great and costs too much. On Saturdays I work in a bike repair shop, fixing punctures and tuning gears. My mum is an accountant and my dad manages an office for a logistics firm, and they cover my rent but I pay for everything else. I'll use an AI chatbot when I'm stuck, but I always check what it tells me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about what I'd bet on. I'd tell my flatmates the hype is always ahead of the reality, and that I'm still glad I learned the stuff properly. At the bike shop my boss Tomasz would say nothing changes there anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the easy scenario for my degree. Software jobs stay roughly as they are, and I can be a normal junior developer in four years. The part that still bothers me is whether I'm good enough, because the maths module has already humbled me, and there's a lot of competition for graduate jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on: lectures, a bit of side coding, and the Saturday shifts. I'd try to get a summer internship at somewhere like my dad's logistics company, since they have an IT department. And I'd keep using the chatbot for stuck moments, but I'd aim to need it less over time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with the normal level of student nerves. The thing keeping me up at night is the maths exam, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the maths module?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the tutor's drop-in session on Wednesdays, which I've been avoiding because it's embarrassing. And I'd do the practice sheets before the lecture, not after. It's boring advice, but it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there's competition for graduate jobs. How do you feel about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reasonably okay. My mum says accountants had the same panic about software in the nineties, and they still had jobs. But I know my degree isn't a guarantee, so I'd rather put in the work early.

say: The hype is always **ahead of the reality**, and I'm glad I learned the stuff properly.
At the bike shop, nothing changes, so I'd say very little.
think: It's the **easy scenario** for my degree: I could be a normal junior developer in four years.
I still doubt whether I'm **good enough**, because the maths module humbled me.
do: Keep up lectures, a bit of **side coding** and the Saturday shifts.
Ask about a **summer internship** at my dad's logistics firm.
Use the chatbot when stuck, but aim to **need it less**.
feel: **Calm**, with normal student nerves; the maths exam keeps me up, not AI.
S0.quote: The thing keeping me up at night is the maths exam, not AI.
fieldNote: A **pragmatist**: judges the scenario by whether it changes his own four-year plan.
Self-doubt about **maths** is a bigger worry than AI in this world.
Uses AI as a **crutch** for stuck moments and wants to rely on it less.

steps.text: Go to the maths tutor's Wednesday drop-in sessions
Do practice sheets before each lecture, not after
Try the chatbot only after attempting problems myself

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, and it's going to be uneven. To flatmates I'd say writing code is going to look different, more like checking and directing. At the bike shop I'd say bikes need hands, so we're fine, which is a bit of a joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, this one is closer to home than I'd like. Entry-level coding is exactly what software does well, so firms might hire fewer juniors, and I'd graduate into a smaller pool of jobs. I'd say there's a 50-50 chance I'd get a proper graduate role in 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the tools more seriously, not only when stuck. I'd build two or three proper projects for my CV, including one that actually works for someone, like a booking system for Tomasz's bike shop. And I'd look at jobs next to software, like IT support or data analysis, and not only developer roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a motivated way. Like a deadline that's real enough to start work on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a booking system for the bike shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's a real problem. Tomasz writes jobs in a notebook, and customers ring up to ask if their bike's ready. I can build it in a month of evenings, and it gives me something to show that isn't a tutorial copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should be responsible if lots of junior jobs vanish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mix. Firms should keep hiring trainees and not only seniors, because otherwise nobody learns. And the government should fund training. I wouldn't want anyone to lean entirely on one side.

At the bike shop I'd joke that bikes need hands, so we're **fine**.

do: Use the tools **seriously**, not only when stuck.

Look at **adjacent jobs** like IT support and data analysis.
feel: **Anxious**, but motivated, like a deadline real enough to start on.
S1.quote: Entry-level coding is exactly what software does well, so firms might hire fewer juniors, and I'd graduate into a smaller pool of jobs.
fieldNote: Judges the **junior coding** squeeze honestly and gives himself even odds of a graduate job.
Turns anxiety into a **real project**: a booking system for the bike shop.
Wants firms to keep hiring **trainees** and government to fund training.

steps.text: Build a booking system for the bike shop
Use AI tools daily to write and test code
Study SQL and data analysis alongside the degree
Support calls for funded graduate training schemes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's hard to take in, and that nobody knows what to do yet. To my flatmates I'd say let's not pretend our degrees are the same as they were, and we should work out what's actually valuable. I wouldn't post anything online, because I'd have no idea what to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be really worried. I'd be in my second year in 2028, with the main thing I'm training for done by software before I finish. I'd feel like the exam changed after I'd started revising. And my mum's accounting and my dad's office job are both desk work, so the whole house is exposed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents quickly about money: how long they can cover my rent if the degree stops making sense, and how much of their own income is at risk. I'd get a second part-time job at the bike shop or a cafe, and I'd put every pound away. I'd stay on the course, because I've got nothing better yet, but I'd also look into apprenticeships in things like rail, electrics or bike mechanics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. I can't sleep on it, and I keep running numbers I don't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't panic, but let's look at what we have. Savings, the mortgage, what each of you could do if your jobs changed. They'd probably laugh at me for being the one with the spreadsheet, but I'd want to be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use the chatbot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, more, probably. If it's going to do everything anyway, I'd rather know what it can and can't do. Better to see it clearly than to be surprised.

S2.quote: I'd feel like the exam changed after I'd started revising.
fieldNote: His **household** is exposed: both parents do desk work, which sharpens his fear.
Offers to make the family **spreadsheet**, so he can be useful.

steps.text: Sit down with my parents to list savings and income
Take a second part-time job at a cafe
Save every spare pound from wages
Look into rail and electrics apprenticeships

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it gives us a bit of time, but nobody should waste it. To flatmates I'd say let's figure out what skills remain valuable, like understanding the problem and talking to the customer. I'd say people should keep their eyes open and not bet everything on one plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the one that feels the most real, because I'd graduate in 2030 and the big change arrives around 2031. I'd have maybe a year in a job. That's not nothing, but it's short, so I'd want to arrive with something extra beyond the degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools every day from now on, to be faster than the people who don't. I'd finish my bike shop booking system and try to sell it to two more shops. I'd also save 2,500 by graduation, which my mum says is about three months of costs. And I'd keep an eye on jobs where a person's name goes on the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious, but it's the kind I can use. It makes me organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different compared with 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 I'd be thinking about whether to drop out. In 2031, I'd finish and try to build a small cushion so I can pick a good job or retrain without being desperate. It's the difference between a flood and a rising river.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who's more worried than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say do one thing this week. Build something, talk to a person who works in the field, or put 50 aside. Doing one thing makes a bigger difference than reading about it all night.

steps.text: Use AI tools every day to build and test code
Sell the booking system to two more bike shops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, and people should use it sensibly. To friends I'd say most of us will change jobs two or three times anyway. I wouldn't be dramatic about it at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fine and a bit curious. I'd be 28 in 2036, and I'd have been working for around six years by then. There's risk, but there's also time to get savings, skills and some options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, take a solid first job, and learn something new every year. I'd put money into a pension and savings early, since compound growth is kind to people who start young. And I'd stay in touch with people from uni, because networks matter when things shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a small, realistic worry. Like knowing there's a hill ahead but also having decent shoes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you worry about your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. They'd be in their late fifties, still working, so the middle years matter for them. I'd quietly check that they're saving and have savings outside of work, because that's what I can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be your main habit for ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learning a bit at a time. Not cramming, not panicking. Pick one skill a year and get decent at it. After ten of those, I'd be hard to replace even by a machine.

say: Ten years is a **long runway**, and people should use it sensibly.
Most of us will change jobs **two or three times** anyway.
think: I'd feel **fine and curious**: 28 in 2036, with six years of work behind me.
There's risk, but there's time to build **savings, skills and options**.
do: Finish the degree and take a **solid first job**, then learn something new every year.
Put money into a **pension** and savings early.
Stay in touch with people from **uni**.
feel: **Mostly calm**, with a small realistic worry, like having decent shoes for a hill.
S4.quote: Pick one skill a year and get decent at it. After ten of those, I'd be hard to replace even by a machine.
fieldNote: Treats ten years as a **runway** for steady habits, not dramatic plans.
Quietly looks out for his **parents'** savings, since they'd still be working.

steps.text: Start a pension contribution with my first job
Learn one new skill every year
Check my parents have savings outside work
Take a solid first job and stay in touch with uni friends

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I'd be only a year in and my whole family is in desk jobs. It's the one where there's no runway. What would help is honest advice about which skills last, a safety net for students, and a way to switch courses without losing a year of money. Also, employers who still hire juniors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really, but I'd say people my age are less lazy and more sensible than they're made out. We use the tools, and we worry about them. We're just trying to find which way to jump.

headlineQuote: People my age are less lazy and more sensible than they're made out.
portrait: Nikhil is an **18-year-old** computer science student, and a pragmatist who works Saturdays at a bike repair shop.
He uses AI **now and then**, checks what it says, and turns worries into projects like a booking system for the shop.
Both his parents do **desk work**, so a fast scenario threatens the whole household, not just his degree.
With more time he plans: **one skill a year**, a cushion, a pension, and quiet checks on his parents' savings.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries him most: no runway, and a whole family in desk jobs.
whatWouldHelp: Honest advice on **which skills last**, a student safety net, switching courses without losing a year, and employers who still hire juniors.
